newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Pakistan has thorny task in reforming state banks.
newsitem.headline: Pakistan has thorny task in reforming state banks.

text.p: Pakistan's caretaker government wants to reform the bloated state financial sector, but faces tough choices over reported World Bank proposals for sweeping staff cutbacks and bank branch closures.

"We are not going to close the bank branches, nor are we going to sack 32,000 people," Shahid Javed Burki, finance and economic affairs adviser to the prime minister, told reporters on Tuesday. He did not elaborate.

Burki was answering a question about a report in the Karachi-based newspaper Business Recorder, which said the World Bank had asked the government to close 20 percent of the 5,085 branches of three state-owned banks and lay off 40 percent of their 80,000 employees by the end of 1996.
It said these were among 21 conditions set by the bank for a proposed $200 million loan to support financial-sector reform.
A World Bank source said the report reflected the broad parameters of bank proposals, but said nothing had been made final and no deadlines had been set for specific actions.
The World Bank had said on November 15 that it was discussing a comprehensive medium-term programme for the reform of the banking sector.
"Implementation of strong reform measures could lay the basis for fast-disbursing financial support by the World Bank," it said in a statement.
Burki is expected to discuss the matter with World Bank officials during talks in Washington next week and a World Bank mission is expected to visit Pakistan this month for further negotiations.

Other reported conditions would tie disbursement of the loan to actual recovery of non-performing loans estimated to total 130 billion rupees ($3.232 billion), as well as legal changes to allow foreclosures and establish more banking courts.
Business Recorder said the World Bank wanted National Bank of Pakistan (NBP), the biggest state-owned bank, to be privatised. The government has said this would not be done.

The World Bank was also reported to have proposed that state-owned Habib Bank Ltd be split into three banks and management stakes sold to private buyers and that Habib Bank's wholly-owned subsidiary Habib Credit and Exchange Bank and state-owned United Bank Ltd also be sold off.

Business Recorder said the World Bank had urged the government to file a court application to liquidate Industrial Development Bank of Pakistan. Other state-run institutions such as the National Development Finance Corporation and the Regional Development Finance Corporation should be downsized and privatised quickly, the World Bank reportedly recommended.
The government has already dissolved the Pakistan Banking Council, another World Bank proposal.
The World Bank was said to have urged the government to ensure that the rate of return on national savings schemes equals the yield given to banks on six-month short-term bonds.

It called for legal changes to strengthen the regulatory and supervisory role of the State Bank of Pakistan, the country's central bank, and minimise the administrative control of the Finance Ministry.
Business Recorder said the government wanted to get the loan approved at a World Bank board meeting on January 21 to allow disbursement before a general election set for February 3.
